name: Femur
func: The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. It carries body weight from the hip to the knee, forms the ball of the hip joint and the top of the knee, and anchors powerful walking and running muscles.

levels.kid:
Your **femur** is your **thigh bone**, the bone inside the top part of your leg, between your hip and your knee.

It's the **longest** and **strongest** bone in your whole body! It's about a quarter of your height. It's so strong it can hold up way more than your body weight.

At the top, it has a round ball that fits into a cup in your hip bone, so your leg can swing forward, backward and out to the side.

At the bottom, it makes the top part of your **knee**, which bends like a hinge.

Big muscles wrap around your femur and help you run, jump, climb stairs and kick a ball. Inside it is soft marrow that helps make your blood!
levels.hs:
The **femur** is the bone of the thigh and the longest, heaviest and strongest bone in the body, roughly a quarter of a person's height.

**Upper end**: the smooth, ball-shaped **head** fits into the **acetabulum** of the hip bone, forming the **hip joint**. The head joins the shaft through an angled **neck**. Where the neck meets the shaft are two large bumps: the **greater trochanter**, which you can feel on the side of your hip, and the **lesser trochanter** on the inner back side. These anchor the hip muscles.

**Shaft**: long and slightly bowed forward. A rough ridge down its back, the **linea aspera**, anchors many thigh muscles.

**Lower end**: it widens into two rounded **condyles** (medial and lateral) that sit on the **tibia** to form the **knee joint**. The **patella** (kneecap) glides in a groove on the front.

The femur slants inward from hip to knee, bringing the knees under the body's centre for balance when walking. The **quadriceps** lies in front, the **hamstrings** behind and the **adductors** on the inner side. The **femoral artery**, a major blood vessel, runs down the front and inner side of the thigh, near the bone.
levels.college:
**Proximal femur**: the **fovea capitis** on the head anchors the **ligament of the head of the femur** (carrying a small artery). The **neck–shaft angle** is about **125°** in adults (larger = **coxa valga**, smaller = **coxa vara**), and the neck is **anteverted** about 10–15° relative to the knee axis. The **intertrochanteric line** (front) and **crest** (back) join the trochanters; the **hip capsule** attaches to the intertrochanteric line in front but only partway down the neck behind.

**Attachments**: **gluteus medius and minimus** on the greater trochanter (hip abductors); **iliopsoas** on the lesser trochanter (main hip flexor); **gluteus maximus** on the **gluteal tuberosity**; adductors and the short head of biceps along the **linea aspera**; **gastrocnemius** heads above the condyles.

**Blood supply of the head**: mostly from **retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery**, running up the neck under the capsule, with small contributions from the lateral circumflex and the artery of the ligament of the head.

**Distal femur**: the condyles are separated behind by the **intercondylar fossa**, where the **cruciate ligaments** attach; the **adductor tubercle** sits above the medial epicondyle.

**Relations**: the **femoral triangle** in the upper thigh contains, from lateral to medial, the **femoral nerve, artery and vein** (and lymphatics in the femoral canal). The femoral artery then runs through the **adductor canal** and becomes the **popliteal artery** behind the knee. The **sciatic nerve** runs behind the femur deep to the hamstrings.
levels.phd:
The femur's internal architecture is the textbook example of form following function. In the proximal femur, trabeculae align with principal stress lines into a **compressive group** (from the head down to the medial cortex) and **tensile group** (arching from the lateral cortex up into the head), leaving a weaker zone between them (**Ward's triangle**). This was the observation behind **Wolff's law**; modern work explains it through osteocyte **mechanotransduction** (fluid shear in canaliculi, sclerostin down-regulation and Wnt/β-catenin signalling) and finite-element models that predict fracture risk from CT data.

The femur grows from a primary diaphyseal centre and secondary centres in the distal end (usually already present at birth), the head (first year), and the greater and lesser trochanters. The **distal femoral physis** is the most active growth plate in the body, contributing about **70%** of femoral length and over a third of total leg length, which is why injuries there can cause significant leg-length differences.

**Femoral neck anteversion** is high in infants (around 30–40°) and decreases during childhood; persistent anteversion causes in-toeing. **Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)** happens in early adolescence during the growth spurt, when the physis is relatively weak in shear; obesity and endocrine factors increase load and weaken the physis.

**Bone marrow**: in children, the femoral shaft is full of red marrow, which converts to fatty yellow marrow from the shaft outward by adulthood, leaving red marrow mainly in the proximal metaphysis, a pattern visible on MRI and important when distinguishing normal marrow from tumour infiltration.
levels.expert:
**Hip (proximal femur) fractures** in older adults usually follow a simple fall: the leg is **shortened and externally rotated**, with pain on moving the hip. **Intracapsular (femoral neck)** fractures can disrupt the medial circumflex femoral blood supply, risking **avascular necrosis** and non-union, so displaced ones are often treated with **hemiarthroplasty** or total hip replacement; **extracapsular (intertrochanteric)** fractures heal well and are fixed with a sliding hip screw or nail. Early surgery and mobilisation improve outcomes.

**Femoral shaft fractures** need high energy in healthy people; they can lose a litre or more of blood into the thigh and are linked to **fat embolism syndrome** (breathing difficulty, confusion, petechial rash). They are usually fixed with an **intramedullary nail**. A shaft fracture from minimal trauma suggests a **pathological fracture** (tumour, metastasis) or atypical fracture.

**Teenage hip problems**: **SCFE** presents with hip, thigh or even only **knee pain** and a limp, with the hip turning outward when flexed; an X-ray (frog-leg lateral view) shows the head slipped like ice cream off a cone (**Klein's line** fails to intersect the head). It is pinned surgically. **Perthes disease** (idiopathic avascular necrosis of the head) affects younger children.

**Osteosarcoma** most often arises in the **distal femur** around the knee in teenagers: a painful swelling with a **sunburst** pattern and **Codman's triangle** on X-ray, confirmed by MRI and biopsy.

**Neurosurgical link**: the **common femoral artery** in the femoral triangle is the classic access route for **cerebral angiography** and endovascular **coiling of brain aneurysms**, though the radial artery is increasingly used. The **femoral nerve** (L2–L4) can be injured by retroperitoneal bleeding.

keyPoints: Longest, strongest bone; ~1/4 of body height
Head + neck + greater/lesser trochanters above; condyles below
Femoral head blood supply mainly from the medial circumflex femoral artery
Hip fracture: shortened, externally rotated leg

test.q: Which artery supplies most of the blood to the femoral head?
test.explain: Its retinacular branches run up the neck, so neck fractures risk avascular necrosis.

test.q: The bump on the side of the hip where gluteus medius attaches is the greater ______.
An older person falls and their leg is shortened and externally rotated. Most likely injury?
test.explain: This is the classic posture of a hip fracture.

test.q: From lateral to medial, the femoral triangle contains:
test.explain: NAV(Y): nerve, artery, vein (and Y for lymphatics) from lateral to medial.

test.q: A 13-year-old with knee pain and a limp whose femoral head has slipped off the neck has slipped capital femoral ______.
test.explain: SCFE occurs in the growth spurt; hip problems can present as knee pain.

test.q: Which bone tumour most often arises around the distal femur in teenagers?
test.explain: Osteosarcoma favours the fast-growing metaphyses around the knee.
